Chief Justice Roberts supphed the crucial fifth vote for Part II-B of the 
Kisor opinion. In his separate concurrence, he declared that “overruling” Auer 
and Seminole Rock was “not warranted” and “agree[d] with the Court’s 
treatment in Part II-B of the bounds of Auer deference.” He remarked that, in 
li&ht of the prerequisites for, and limitations on, Auer deference” announced 
by Kisor, the distance between the majority and Justice Gorsuch is not as 
great as it may initially appear.” That statement appeared to discount the 
differences between the approaches in Kisor and Skidmore. At the same timp^ 
he claimed Auer deference is not “just the same as the power of persuasion 
discussed in Skidmore, because “there is a difference between holding that a 
court ought to be persuaded by an agency’s interpretation and holding that it 
should defer to that interpretation under certain conditions.” That fitatement 
echoed the distinction between “respect” for, and “deference” to, agency 
interpretations that Chief Justice Roberts employed in Loper Bright—albeit, 
in that case, to overrule Chevron deference. Notably, in his Kisor concurrence, 
Chief Justice Roberts said that he did “not regard the Court’s decision today to 
touch upon” Chevron.
In Loper Bright, Chief Justice Roberts did not cast doubt on Kisor. As of 
the time of this writing, both Loper Bright and Kisor remain good law.
2. 
Auer Deference and the APA. For a plurality of the Court, Justice 
Kagan argued at length that Auer deference is consistent with the APA. Chief 
Justice Roberts did not join this part of Justice Kagan’s opinion, and his 
majority opinion in Loper Bright appears to embrace a different understanding 
of Section 706.
